blocks.p: Dear Stephen, read the part about seventy times seven again. Then put the book down and try the arithmetic on someone. You will find you cannot get past about four. I am told that is the point.
There was no one to bury on Viper, so they buried no one, and wept anyway.

They did it in the canteen of Cinder Station, eight days after the crawlers came. The station’s people had heard the beacon on the second day and come for them on the third, six squat machines grinding across the black plain in a line, their lamps swinging, and the miners who climbed down out of them had wrapped the survivors in their own coats and given them their own bunks and asked nothing. Pim had told the story of the adder in the first crawler, and by the time they reached the station everyone there had heard it. Some of the miners looked at Sol’s face the way Pim had. He told every one of them that he was an old man with a sore hand, and they nodded, and went on looking.

Lyda had asked for the service. She was on her feet by then, just, with three of her ribs cracked from Sol’s hands and a dressing on her chest from Lucan’s pads, and she sat in the front of the canteen in a borrowed miner’s jacket with her back very straight, because it hurt less that way. Teo sat beside her. On the table in front of them, because there was nothing else, were three things the crawlers had found in the wreck: Corwin Brack’s cap, which he had left on a hook in the forward hold; a tin whistle Ina Moss had used to start the songs on the gangway; and the pressure gauge Fenn had shown Sol how to read, which had come loose from its housing in the landing.

The believers from the Petrel sat together. There were eleven of them. Around them, along the walls and in the doorway, the miners of Cinder Station stood and watched, the way people might watch an animal they had heard of and never seen.

Sol read from the grey notebook. He had chosen it before he knew he was choosing, the way the psalm had come by the fire. A man’s friend had died, and his sisters had sent for him, and he had come too late. I am the resurrection and the life, he read. Whoever believes in me, even though he dies, will live, and everyone who lives and believes in me will never die. (John 11:25–26) He read on, past the sisters and their reproach, to the grave cut in the rock, and the two words that Stephen had once said in a cell on Serenity, lying back on his cot like an old man in an archival image. He wept.
He had to stop there for a while. No one minded.

Lyda did not weep. She sat with her hands around Ina’s whistle and her jaw set and her eyes on the gauge, and it was Teo who broke, and Tobin, and two women who had been bound for Galatia, and then, to Sol’s surprise, a man along the wall: the renewed miner from the forward rows of the hold, the one who had looked away. He stood with his untouched face wet and his mouth working, staring at his own fingers as though they had betrayed him. No one went to him. Sol did not think he would have known what to do if they had.
Afterward, when the canteen had emptied, Lyda stayed where she was.
“Did he go up?” she said. “Corwin. He was renewed. He went to the Pearl every rest day for thirty years, for his wife. Did he go up to her?”
“I don’t know,” Sol said.
“You were a bishop.”

“Yes. That’s how I know I don’t know.” He looked at the cap on the table. “And because I sat in Lucan’s cellar while Teo listened. Every rest day for thirty years her Pearl told Corwin she was happy. I don’t know what she was saying under it. If he went up to her, he knows now.”

It was all he had: one boy on one cot. Lucan had never found his second listener. No one with a live Halo would let a heretic’s wire near it, and after the cellar he would not put one in another dark head, so he had stopped asking.

She looked at him then. Her eyes were very dark in her pale face, and dry, and he thought she was going to be angry, and found that he would have welcomed it. But she only nodded once, as if he had told her the price of something, and turned Ina’s whistle over in her fingers.
“At least you don’t lie,” she said. “I’ll give you that. You never did.”
Teo and Lucan came for him that night.

They had been shut in the station’s little infirmary for six days with the nav core, which Teo had wired to an old diagnostic board of the station’s, and which now sat on the examining table under a lamp like a patient. Lucan had his spectacles on his nose and a page of his notebook covered with columns. Teo had not slept; Sol could see it in the set of his mouth and the bruised look under his eyes, and he watched the boy’s hands for the small tremor that sometimes came before one of his spells. They were steady. Lyda came in behind Sol without being asked and sat on the edge of the cot.

“Before Teo starts,” Lucan said, “I owe Lyda a result.” He did not look at her; he looked at his columns. “I read the implant’s log through the station’s board. It did what it was built to do. When the pod lost power it held your heart at the stasis rate for as long as the pod stayed cold. But the lid had cracked, and the cold went out of it in minutes instead of hours, faster than the pulse was ever meant to carry a heart through. It held the rhythm as long as it could, and then it lost it, and you went with it.” He turned a page. “Without it you would have been dead long before the hold came down.”
“And the door,” Lyda said. “The one he burned.”

“Had nothing to do with it. I checked that first.” Lucan looked up at last. “Nothing can write to the one in your head now, not even me, and I find I’m glad of that. So I’ve changed the pod instead: a second lid, and a warming governor of my own that will bring you up slowly whatever the ship does around it.”

“A crossing that long is two folds, not one,” Teo said. “You know that. A drive spends itself on every fold, and one charge only reaches so far. So halfway the ship comes out, lies quiet a few hours while the drive charges again, takes a fix, and folds the rest of the way. You always put the turn in empty space. Nothing for a light-year in any direction. That’s the whole art of it.” He touched the board, and a chart opened above it, faint lines in the lamplight. “This is the route Brack filed at Philippa. The turn’s here. Empty.” He touched it again. “This is the route we flew.”

The second line bent. It ran off the first at a shallow angle, and its turn fell in a small system off to one side: a dim red star, a banded giant, a scatter of dust around the giant like a ring of grit, and a moon.

“The amendment came in forty minutes before we left the pier,” Teo said. “It put the turn right inside the Coil’s debris belt. The Scatter, Pim calls it. Nobody drops out in the Scatter. There’s a hazard notice on it in every Thorne chart I’ve ever seen.” His voice tightened. “It isn’t on this one. Whoever sent the amendment took it off.”
“Brack would have argued,” Lyda said.

“Not with this.” Lucan turned his notebook toward her. “The amendment came through the port chaplaincy. Every ship clearing Philippa files with the chaplain; Thorne ships too, as Lyda knows better than I. Most amendments are his own, and Brack would have argued with Ferrin until his face went purple. This one was not Ferrin’s. Ferrin only relayed it. It carried a higher authority.” He laid one finger on the column. “An episcopal office. Sion.”
The infirmary was quiet. Somewhere in the station a pump started and ran and stopped.
“Which bishop?” Sol said.

“It does not say. It gives the office’s mark, not the man’s.” Lucan took his spectacles off and folded them. “But there are not so many offices that could reach out this far. And there is something else.” He looked at Teo.
Teo reached into his jacket and brought out a flat grey wafer, the kind the ships carried mail in, sealed at one edge with a thin line of white.

“The Petrel carried a dispatch packet for Galatia,” he said. “Church post, mostly, and Thorne business. This was in it. It came aboard through the chaplaincy in the same hour as the amendment, under the same mark.” He held it out. “It’s addressed to you. I didn’t open it.”

Sol took it. His name was on the seal, in the formal script of the episcopate: Sol Tarren, Bishop of Life. It had been a long time since anyone had written that. He broke the seal with his thumbnail, and the wafer warmed in his hand and opened its page in the air above it. It was not script. It was a page of handwriting, put down on paper and copied into the wafer, and he knew the hand before he had read a word of it: the same labored, careful loops he had teased him for on the panel.
Tarren,
They tell me you are crossing to Galatia on a Thorne ship called the Petrel. I won’t tell you who told me. I won’t tell you what else they tell me, or how often.
I have asked for your road to be changed. It was the only thing I could do. If the ship’s people argue, don’t let them. For once in your life, Tarren, don’t argue.
You asked me the right questions. I have not stopped asking them. That is the whole of the trouble.
Whatever you hear of me after this, I did love you. Go with Life.

He read it twice. Then he held it out, and Lucan read it, and Teo read it over Lucan’s shoulder, and then Lyda held out her hand for it, and read it, and set it down on the cot beside her very carefully, as if it might go off.

“He killed them,” Teo said. His voice cracked. “He knew which ship. He had the turn moved into the Scatter. He killed Corwin and Ina and Fenn, and he tried to kill you, and he wrote you a letter to say he loved you while he did it.”
“Perhaps,” Lucan said.
“Perhaps?”

“I am a doctor, Teo. I am paid to read symptoms, and symptoms lie.” Lucan put his spectacles back on, as though he needed them to think. “There are two ways to read this, and I cannot tell you which is true. In one, Bishop Croft is told that Tarren is on the Petrel, and he arranges for the Petrel not to arrive, and he writes to say goodbye. In the other, Bishop Croft is told that something is waiting for Tarren at Galatia, and he asks for the ship to be sent another way, and someone else, someone who knows how to take a hazard notice off a chart, decides what the other way will be.” He spread his hands. “It was the only thing I could do. That is either a confession or a man saying that he tried. The letter does not know which it is. I am not sure the man who wrote it did either.”
“You believe that?” Lyda said. Her voice was flat.
“I believe I do not know,” Lucan said. “I am writing it down that way.”

“Then write down a third thing.” Lyda picked up the wafer again and turned it over. “He tells you not to let the ship’s people argue. That’s a letter you read before you sail. And it came aboard sealed in the Galatia packet, in the hold, with you asleep in a pod above it. I run the post on that line. Nobody puts a warning where the man can’t read it until he’s landed.” She set it down. “Unless he doesn’t know how the post runs. Or somebody else does.”
Lucan wrote it down.
Lyda turned to Sol. “And you?”

Sol did not answer. He was thinking of the residence line in his study at Concord, voice only, and Aurelian’s voice on it, warm and quick and trying very hard to sound as it always sounded. I’ll sign it at the evening office. I have to. You understand that I have to. He had signed. Sol had always known he would have; it was why he had given Sol the hours before it. He was thinking, too, of something worse: the panel in the Thorne office, the last minute of the quarter hour, and his own voice. Daphne in the spring, I think, and then Galatia. And at the far end of the dark office Lyda had lifted her head. Knowing where a man is and knowing where he’s going are different things.
“I told him,” he said. “I told him I was going.”
“You told him a season,” Lucan said. “You didn’t tell him a ship. Somebody did.”

Lyda had gone still on the cot. “Weir,” she said. “Ferrin takes the route, and Weir takes the souls. Every sailing list on the river goes into his registry before the ship can clear, and up the line the same day. The Petrel’s went in a week before she sailed, with your name on it.” Her mouth thinned. “I bought my brother off that registry. I didn’t buy you off it. He told me to my face I couldn’t.”
“Up through Weir and back down through Ferrin,” Lucan said. “The filings would have told them, Tarren, whatever you said on that panel.”

Sol knew it was true. It did not help. He had said Galatia into a brass grille to a frightened man, and the weight of it did not care whether it had been needed. He did not put it down. It was his, whoever else had done the work.

He went out to the viewport at the end of the station’s long corridor, where the miners went to smoke their bitter Viper leaf and watch the Coil, and he stood there alone with the letter in his hand while the shadow came across the plain. He watched the plumes of steam go grey and go out, one by one, and the black sand go blacker, and the cold came against the glass in front of his face and stayed there.
He signed, the voice said.

It was very quiet this time. It did not shout. It spoke in his own voice, at the level of his own thinking, and the crackle under it was so faint he could almost have missed it. He signed it at the evening office, and he signed this, and he will sign the next one. He was always going to. You knew it at Concord. You have known it for four hundred years. You know his face better than your own, and you know there is nothing behind it. A pause, like a breath. Go back and ask him. Go back to Sion and stand in front of him and ask him to his face. You’ll know then. You’ll know. Go back.
“Christ,” Sol said.
The voice broke at the name, as it always did. The feeling did not. What was left when the voice had gone was worse, because it was his own.

He was angry. He had not known he could be, not like this. Renewal had taken anger from him so many times that he had come to think of it as something that happened to other people, in the archival images, red faces and open mouths. Now it rose in him like heat from a fissure. He thought of Ina Moss laughing at Teo on the gangway. He thought of Lyda’s face the color of candle wax, and the small soft crack under the heel of his hand. He thought of Aurelian in some warm room in Sion, with the letter gone and the thing done, touching his temple to open the evening’s forms, and he wanted, with a want so plain it frightened him, for Aurelian to be on the other side of this glass, out there in the cold, and to know what it was.
He stood with that for a long time. He did not pray it away. He did not think he could have.
Then, because he did not know what else to do, he opened the grey notebook.

He did not look for anything. It fell open where it had been opened most, early in the first Gospel, where Stephen’s hand had pressed hardest into the paper and the letters stood up like braille. It was the prayer. Sol had read it aloud in every house church from Daphne to Ephes. He had taught it to Teo line by line on the pier at Philippa. He had never once, he realized now, read it as though it were addressed to him.
Forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors. (Matt. 6:12)
He read it again.

Then, because the notebook was in his hands and his hands knew the way, he turned to the end of the third Gospel, where the man they had nailed up looked down at the men who had done it, and said, Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing. (Luke 23:34)
They do not know what they are doing. Lucan had said it in his clinic voice an hour ago. I am not sure the man who wrote it did either.

And he thought, suddenly and with complete clarity, of a white room on Serenity with a needle in it. Of an old man on a narrow bed with the wardens’ calm hands on him, not looking at the wardens. Looking past Sol, to someone Sol could not see. Do not hold this against him. (Acts 7:60)

He had signed for Stephen. In the Bounty Market, and again in that white room, on the line Kell held out to him. He had signed, and been sure he was doing a kindness, and he had not known what he was doing; and Stephen had known that he did not know, and had asked for him anyway, at the end, with what breath he had left.

Sol stood at the glass with the notebook open in his hands, and the anger did not go. That surprised him most, afterward. He had thought forgiveness would come like the sight back into his eyes, all at once, in flakes. It did not come at all. He had to go and get it. He had to decide it, standing in the cold with his hand still sore and his heart still hot, and say it aloud to the empty corridor, and know as he said it that he would have to say it again in the morning, and the morning after that, and perhaps every morning for the rest of his life.
“I forgive him,” he said. “Whatever he did. Whatever he knew. I forgive him.” And then, because it was true, and because he was learning not to say what was not: “Help me mean it tomorrow.”
He wrote the letter that night, at the canteen table, by the light of a miner’s lamp, with Lucan asleep in a chair against the wall and his little book open on his chest.

Aurelian. The Petrel broke up in the Scatter off Viper. Corwin Brack, Ina Moss, and a man called Fenn are dead. A woman I love was dead for nine minutes on a deck. I have your letter. I don’t know what you did. I don’t know whether you know what you did. If you did anything, I forgive you. I will have to forgive you again tomorrow, I expect, and I will. Stephen Hale forgave me for more. The questions are good questions. Keep asking them. You can come out here, if you want to. It’s far, and they don’t come. They send. Sol.
He looked at the last word a long while. Aurelian had never once used it.

The Kestrel came for them nineteen days later, down through the brown sky on a column of fire. Her master was the narrow, unsmiling woman who had closed Sol’s lid on Plenty. She took the letter from him on the ramp without looking at the address, and put it inside her jacket, and said she would see it as far as Plenty, and from Plenty it would find its own way.
“Thorne ships don’t ask,” she said.
Lyda was waiting for him at the top of the ramp, one hand held against her ribs. She had been there, he understood, the whole time. She had heard.
“You don’t get to forgive him for Corwin,” she said. “Or Ina. That isn’t yours.”
“No,” Sol said. “Only my part.”
“And my part?”
“That’s yours.”
She looked at him for a long moment, with the black plain behind her and the Coil turning overhead. Then she held out her hand.
“Give me the book,” she said. “Not the reading. Not you reading it to me in a room full of people. The book.” Her mouth tightened. “I want to see for myself what it is that makes a man do that.”
